Every single module fits comfortably inside a single 46 KB read_file call with zero truncation!

5. Act IV: From Prompt Scars to "Zero-Token, Zero-Turn" AST Auto-Fixes (package:synthetic_scars_lint)

Ctbhatia's Challenge: "Otherwise It Is the Callsite Test with a Longer Name"

In our r/AI_Agents thread, Ctbhatia asked a pointed question about what happens after we codify a scar from a production bug:

"If a scar only lives in a unit test for the file that broke—or in a markdown doc that an agent has to remember to read—what happens six weeks later when the agent creates a brand-new file (new_feature_modal.dart) and repeats the exact same structural bug? Unless the lock automatically sweeps every newly created file in the repository, a 'class lock' is just a callsite test with a longer name."

Ctbhatia nailed it. And that observation sparked our biggest engineering leap since the Makefile: package:synthetic_scars_lint—graduating Synthetic Scars out of Markdown prompts and into deterministic compiler AST rules with 15ms dart fix auto-remediation.

Why Standard Linters (flutter_lints) Fail AI Coding Agents

Wait—doesn't Dart already have dart analyze and flutter_lints? Why not just turn on standard lints?

Because standard linters were written to police human habits, whereas AI agents fail by inventing clever linter-evasion local minima!

Look back at TICKET-482 (SCAR-RIV-14) from Part 3.11. In Flutter, if you write ScaffoldMessenger.of(context).showSnackBar(...) after an await gap, the built-in use_build_context_synchronously lint yells at you.

How does a frontier LLM silence that lint warning? Instead of checking if (!context.mounted) return; after the await, the LLM hoists the lookup above the await:

// ❌ THE LLM LINTER-EVASION TRAP (SCAR-RIV-14):
// Silences `use_build_context_synchronously`, but crashes or leaks when the modal
// sheet unmounts during `await saveForm()`!
Future<void> onSubmit(BuildContext context) async {
  final messenger = ScaffoldMessenger.of(context); // <-- Hoisted before await!
  final l10n = AppLocalizations.of(context);       // <-- Hoisted before await!
  await saveForm();
  // ZERO `if (!context.mounted) return;` check here!
  messenger.showSnackBar(SnackBar(content: Text(l10n.savedMessage)));
}

The built-in Dart linter gives that code zero warnings (No issues found!) because context wasn't lexically passed after the await. The LLM defeated the human linter—while leaving the production runtime crash wide open!

The 3-Stage Scar Cost Collapse (From Thousands of Tokens to 0 Tokens and 0 Turns)

Once a failure mode is structurally well-defined (like SCAR-RIV-14 pre-captured context handles across await, SCAR-AST-07 RecursiveAstVisitor leaf vacuity, or SCAR-ASYNC-09 unawaited stream teardowns), keeping it in a Markdown file forever is like hiring a security guard to read a sticky note instead of installing a circuit breaker.

By graduating deterministic scars into package:synthetic_scars_lint (plugged straight into Dart's analysis_server_plugin / custom_lint pipeline), a scar evolves through three stages:

Lifecycle Stage Where the Scar Lives Up-Front Prompt Token Cost Cost When the Agent Makes the Mistake Sweeps Brand-New Files Automatically?
Stage 1: Markdown Prompt Scar references/09_stack_*.md (insmod module) ~150–300 tokens per mounted scar 1 full Target 40 -> 30 Critic bounce (15–30 seconds + ~8,000 LLM tokens) Only if the subagent mounts and heeds the prompt
Stage 2: Compiler Diagnostic Scar (Sensor?Receipt) package:synthetic_scars_lint (AnalysisRule + LintCode) 0 prompt tokens (retired from Markdown!) 1 local worker turn (dart analyze prints the 3-part [SCAR-ID] Wound / Trap / Reflex at the exact line:col) Yes (100% of .dart files in dart analyze)
Stage 3: AST Auto-Fix Scar (dart fix --apply) package:synthetic_scars_lint (ResolvedCorrectionProducer) 0 prompt tokens 0 LLM turns (~15 milliseconds) (dart fix --apply splices the guard straight into the AST!) Yes (100% automatic AST repair)

Look at Stage 2 and Stage 3:

  • When the agent is writing clean code that doesn't trigger SCAR-RIV-14, the scar costs 0 tokens of prompt context because it no longer lives in Markdown.
  • If the agent writes the hoisted final messenger = ScaffoldMessenger.of(context); trap in a brand-new file at Target 30, Stage 2 catches the AST pattern inside dart analyze (Sensor?Receipt) and emits the exact 3-part Scar diagnostic ([SCAR-RIV-14] Pre-captured BuildContext handle used after await without context.mounted guard).
  • Even better, for Stage 3 scars with a canonical local fix, running dart fix --apply && dart analyze in the Target 30 pre-flight script invokes our ResolvedCorrectionProducer, which splices if (!context.mounted) return; directly after the await node in 15 milliseconds without burning a single LLM retry turn!
  • And what happens to the old Markdown paragraph in references/09_stack_flutter_and_web_ui.md? Once the AST rule and its negative witness test (// expect_lint: scar_riv_14) pass in CI, the Markdown prompt entry undergoes Scar Apoptosis—physically retired to a 1-line tombstone (Lifecycle: Graduated -> package:synthetic_scars_lint), keeping our prompt modules permanently lean.

Ctbhatia's Torture-Tree Benchmark Triad: Keeping 500 AST Rules Under < 1 ms

When I proposed moving hundreds of scars into AST visitors, Ctbhatia raised the next systems concern:

"If you add 100 custom AST rules, and a rule author accidentally writes a visitor callback that walks .parent pointers up to the compilation unit root—or compares sibling nodes pairwise—won't dart analyze grind to a quadratic O(N^2) halt on large Flutter widget trees?"

Yes—if each rule traverses the AST separately or walks .parent chains inside deep leaves!

First, Dart's RuleVisitorRegistry uses single-pass AST sharing: the analyzer parses each .dart file into an AST once and dispatches node events (addMethodInvocation, addAwaitExpression, addSwitchStatement) across registered rules in a single walk (< 1 ms per rule when each callback is O(1)).

Second, to make sure no quadratic O(D^2), O(W^2), or O(D * W) visitor ever sneaks into package:synthetic_scars_lint, my peer-review exchange with Ctbhatia produced the Torture-Tree Benchmark Triad:

flowchart TD
    Root["📐 The Torture-Tree Benchmark Triad\n(Deterministic AST Step-Count Gate: Steps / N ≤ C)"]
    S1["1. The Tall Spine (D = 50, W = 1)\n50-level nested single-child chain\nCatches: O(D²) un-memoized depth recursion"]
    S2["2. The Wide Comb (D = 1, W = 1,000)\n1 container with 1,000 sibling nodes\nCatches: O(W²) pairwise sibling scans"]
    S3["3. The Broom Tree (D = 30 × W = 500)\n30-level deep stalk ending in 500 leaves\nCatches: O(D × W) leaf .parent walks (15,000 hops!)"]

    Root --> S1
    Root --> S2
    Root --> S3

Why do you need all three tree shapes in CI?

  • 1. The Tall Spine (D = 50, W = 1): A 50-level deeply nested single-child widget chain. Catches un-memoized depth recursion (O(D^2)), but completely misses sibling fan-out bugs.
  • 2. The Wide Comb (D = 1, W = 1,000): A single container at depth 1 with 1,000 sibling expressions. Catches O(W^2) pairwise sibling scans—but completely masks .parent pointer walks, because at depth D = 1, walking .parent to the root only takes 1 hop!
  • 3. The Broom Tree (D = 30 × W = 500): A 30-level deep single-child stalk terminating in a 500-child wide brush at the bottom. If a leaf callback walks .parent pointers up to the compilation unit root, it looks harmless on the Wide Comb (500 × 1 = 500 hops) and harmless on the Tall Spine (1 × 50 = 50 hops), but explodes multiplicatively on the Broom Tree (500 × 30 = 15,000 pointer hops)!

And instead of relying on noisy wall-clock timers in CI (where Dart VM JIT warm-up hides algorithmic regressions), the Torture-Tree Triad asserts directly on deterministic AST visitor step counts per node:

Total Visitor Steps / N_AST_Nodes <= C

If any contributor writes a rule that walks .parent chains or scans siblings quadratically, the normalized step ratio blows past C on the Broom Tree and fails the test deterministically on any CPU.

6. Summary: Why the Best Prompt Rule Is the One You Delete—And Onward to Part 4

Look at the arc from Part 3.6 to Part 3.12:

  • In Part 3.6, I stopped writing 20-step English checklists and gave the agent a 1976 Makefile DAG.
  • In Part 3.7, I stopped trusting context windows and put state in 1983 /etc/init.d files with fork()/wait() subagents.
  • In Part 3.8, I proved across 1,680 controlled A/B trials that 50-year-old CS formalisms (Makefile, init.d, EBNF, Design-by-Contract, 2PC, Circuit Breakers, git bisect) tap into massive pre-training gravity.
  • In Part 3.9 and Part 3.10, I replaced 130 lines of defensive "Do NOT..." prompt lawyering with Fernando Flores's 1986 Committed Speech (Request, Promise, Assertion, Declaration) and Nuel Belnap's 4-valued truth lattice.
  • In Part 3.11, I flight-tested that machine across 926+ production steps, two context lobotomies, a mid-flight vendor swap, and an open-weight crash test.
  • And here in Part 3.12, peer review from systems engineers, compiler writers, and an autonomous AI proved the ultimate law of prompt engineering: the best prompt rule is the one you delete by pushing it down into an unforgeable sensor:
    • Delete "don't cheat on tests" from the prompt → Enforce Two-Layer Native git write-tree Merkle Locks and Read-Only test/ Pins across Red -> Green.
    • Delete "don't bail out lazily" from the prompt → Enforce a 3-Part Scoped Counter-Witness Receipt backed by compiler symbol resolution.
    • Delete 280 KB of monolithic scar prose → Mount <36 KB stack slices on demand via git diff Linux insmod Loadable Scar Modules (09_failure_vaccines.md).
    • Delete graduated domain scars from Markdown altogether → Compile them into package:synthetic_scars_lint + dart fix --apply, repairing the AST in 15ms at a cost of 0 prompt tokens and 0 LLM retry turns.

back, when what I wanted was a teacher looking over my shoulder: circle the mistake, tick what's right, nudge me toward
the next step, and show me why. penmentor is that, one key away, on my own Claude subscription.

How it helps you learn

  • Hints, not answers. A ladder from a nudge to naming the technique to a faint ghost of the next line: you do the thinking, which is what makes it stick.
  • Feedback on your own work. The first real mistake circled where you made it, correct lines ticked, later lines that inherit the mistake underlined. The marks stay while you keep writing; Esc clears them.
  • Practice that makes you recall. Questions on your key steps (answer by typing or by writing), find-the-error drills, "which technique fits?".
  • See it. Box what you want to understand and get an interactive animation made with 3Blue1Brown's own manim: drag the bounds, retype a value, watch Riemann sums close in.
  • Whole page aware. A small xournal++ plugin shares the page you are on, not just what fits on screen.

Works with Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity

penmentor runs on the AI command-line agent you already use, on that subscription. Pick the model in Settings; its
prefix says which agent answers:

Prefix Agent For example
claude: Claude Code claude:opus, claude:sonnet, claude:haiku
codex: Codex codex:gpt-5.6-terra
agy: Antigravity CLI agy:gemini-4-argon-medium, agy:gemini-3.8-flash-medium

Settings lists the agents you have installed. How each one is run and what it sees: the guide.

Quick start 

git clone https://github.com/AbdullahAlhariri/penmentor ~/src/penmentor
~/src/penmentor/bin/penmentor --selftest

Linux on X11 (best with i3), with one of those agents logged in (claude, codex or agy), plus rofi, slop,
xdotool and PyQt6. Bind bin/penmentor to a key (example). Setup, keys and how it works: the guide.

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Every codebase I've touched has the same line in it:

<img src="/imgs/cookie.png" alt="" />

It's rarely because we don't care about accessibility. Describing forty images is just the most boring job in front-end, so it gets pushed to "later."

So I built a VS Code extension that does it for me. Hover over any <img> with a missing or empty alt, click Generate alt text, and the description is written straight into your code.

Feeling really lazy? Press Cmd+Shift+A (Ctrl+Shift+A on Windows/Linux) and it fills in every empty alt in the file at once.

A few small rules keep it safe to trust:

  • It never overwrites alt text you already wrote.
  • Failures are reported per image, and the successful ones are still applied.
  • Output is escaped, so a stray quote can't break your markup.

Code

0shuvo0 / ai-img-alt-text-ext

Generate accessible image alt text in HTML, JSX, and TSX files using a locally running Ollama vision model. Image contents are sent only to the Ollama server you configure.

AI Image Alt Text

Generate accessible image alt text in HTML, JSX, and TSX files using a locally running Ollama vision model. Image contents are sent only to the Ollama server you configure.

Features

  • Hover over an <img> element with an empty or missing alt attribute and select Generate alt text.
  • Press Cmd+Shift+A (or Ctrl+Shift+A on Windows/Linux) to fill empty or missing alt attributes in the current file.
  • Supports multiline tags, other attributes, workspace-relative image files, and HTTP(S) image URLs.
  • Existing non-empty alt text is never overwritten. Bulk generation reports individual image failures and applies successful results together.

Requirements

  • Ollama running locally or at a server you can access.

  • A vision-capable model installed in Ollama, for example:

    ollama pull gemma3:latest

The first generation prompts for the Ollama server URL (for example http://localhost:11434) and model name. These values are saved in the VS Code user settings. To change them…


View on GitHub


How I Built It

The whole thing runs on Gemma 3 through Ollama, entirely on my own machine.

When you click the button, the extension:

  1. Finds the image. It checks the workspace root first, then common static folders like public/, so /imgs/cookie.png just works. Remote URLs work too.
  2. Sends it to the local Gemma model with a short prompt asking for a concise, useful description.
  3. Writes the result back into the alt attribute.

Setup is two steps: ollama pull gemma3:latest, then point the extension at your Ollama URL. The model name is a setting, so you can swap in any other vision model without touching the code.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Alt text feels like a perfect job for a hosted API, until you think about what you'd be sending it.

Your images stay yours. Client mockups, unreleased products and internal dashboards often sit in a repo long before anyone should see them. With a local model, nothing leaves the laptop.

It costs nothing per image. A big project can have hundreds of images. Running them through Gemma costs electricity, not a bill that grows with your codebase.

It's swappable. If a better open vision model shows up next month, it's a one-line settings change. I'm not tied to one provider's pricing or availability.

The honest trade-off: a local model is slower than a hosted API. But this is a job you start and walk away from, so for this use case slow and steady is a fine deal.

The Lazy Payoff

I ran it on 20 images from one of my projects.

  • Time: just 3 minutes, versus roughly 10 minutes writing them by hand.
  • Usable as-is: 18 out of 20 descriptions needed no editing.
  • Where it struggled: Animated or vector images eg gif files

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma: every description is generated by Gemma 3, running locally through Ollama.

articles.title: What If the Next Operating System Had No Apps? The Future of Intent-Native Computing
articles.description: What If the Next Operating System Had No Apps?   The Future of Computing Might Not Be...
articles.body_html:
What If the Next Operating System Had No Apps?

The Future of Computing Might Not Be Applications, but Intent.

We have spent decades improving software.

Faster applications. Better programming languages. More powerful operating systems. Increasingly intelligent AI assistants.

But there is one fundamental assumption we rarely question:

Why do humans have to choose the applications before computers can understand what they want to accomplish?

Think about it.

You want to create a video, so you open a video editor.

You want to analyze information, so you open a spreadsheet.

You want to build software, so you open an IDE.

You want to automate a workflow, so you connect several different tools.

The computer has enormous processing power, yet much of the responsibility for organizing the work still belongs to us.

What if we reversed that relationship?

The Radical Idea: Software Generated Around Intent

Imagine entering this request:

"Take my project folder, analyze its architecture, identify potential problems, create a dependency visualization, and generate a report."

A conventional workflow might require several applications, scripts, and manual steps.

An intent-native computer could approach the problem differently.

First, it understands the objective.

Then it identifies the required capabilities.

Next, it creates an execution plan, requests the necessary permissions, and assembles an interface for the task.

The result isn't necessarily a newly installed application.

It might be a temporary workspace built from existing reusable components.

The Architecture Behind the Idea

Conceptually, such a system might have six layers:

  1. Intent interpretation: Translate the user's request into a structured objective.
  2. Planning: Identify dependencies, constraints, and necessary capabilities.
  3. Permission management: Ensure each operation is authorized.
  4. Capability execution: Run existing tools, libraries, and services.
  5. Dynamic interface composition: Present controls appropriate to the task.
  6. Verification and recovery: Record outcomes, surface uncertainty, and support rollback where possible.

A request could be represented like this:

{
  "intent": "analyze_project",
  "source": "./my-project",
  "requirements": [
    "dependency_graph",
    "architecture_report",
    "security_review"
  ],
  "execution": {
    "preferLocal": true,
    "networkAccess": false,
    "requireApprovalForChanges": true
  }
}

This example is a conceptual specification, not a working operating-system API.

Notice something important: the request describes the desired result and its constraints, not a particular application.

Does This Mean Traditional Apps Will Disappear?

Not necessarily.

Applications are valuable because they offer predictable workflows, specialized interfaces, and mature functionality.

Professional video editors, CAD tools, debuggers, and scientific software cannot simply be replaced by a text box.

But perhaps the long-term opportunity is to make applications optional entry points rather than mandatory boundaries.

Developers could expose individual capabilities.

Users could combine them.

AI could assist with translating goals into safe, inspectable workflows.

The Hardest Problem Isn't Intelligence

It's trust.

Suppose a computer understands the instruction:

"Clean up my project."

Does that authorize deleting files?

Renaming folders?

Changing dependencies?

Uploading source code to a remote service?

Of course not.

An intent-native system would need explicit capability boundaries, permission checks, reversible operations where feasible, and reliable records of what actually executed.

It must also distinguish an AI-generated plan from an operation that genuinely ran.

Otherwise, we would merely replace application complexity with automation risk.

Could This Work Without the Cloud?

At least parts of it could.

A local-first implementation might combine:

  • On-device language models for interpreting requests.
  • A deterministic execution engine for carrying out approved operations.
  • Sandboxed components for isolated capabilities.
  • Local storage for user data and execution history.
  • Optional cloud services when explicitly authorized.

The difficult engineering work would be making these parts reliable, secure, interoperable, and efficient.

The Bigger Question

What if the most important innovation in computing isn't another operating system feature?

What if it's changing what an operating system considers its fundamental unit of work?

Today, we primarily organize computing around applications, windows, files, and processes.

Perhaps future systems could also organize computing around goals, capabilities, permissions, and verified outcomes.

That wouldn't eliminate programming.

It could create entirely new opportunities for programming language designers, operating-system engineers, and developers building reusable software components.

Maybe the future of computing isn't choosing the right application.

Maybe it's describing the result you want—and having the computer safely assemble the tools to get there.

This remains a vision, not a solved engineering problem.

But I think it's a question worth exploring.

Developers: Would you use an operating system built around intentions instead of applications? Or do traditional applications offer something we should never give up?

Exploring the future of systems programming, local-first software, AI engineering, and developer tools.

Website: https://sanskarin.github.io

articles.title: SlothVault: A Zero-Effort Local MCP + RAG Agent That Rewards Digital Laziness published: true
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady          ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

SlothVault is a local-first personal RAG utility built for anyone too tired or busy to manually sort, tag, and organize digital clutter.

Every day, developers and researchers accumulate messy context fragments:

  • Home lab and Wi-Fi credentials
  • Cloud subscription renewal dates and invoice amounts
  • Medical appointments and task deadlines

Most productivity guides advise spending hours building complex databases in Notion or Obsidian. SlothVault takes the lazy approach: dump your unorganized notes into a local vault and let an open-weight agent fetch what you need in seconds.

  1. Zero Manual Tagging: It ingests raw notes, credentials, and .txt files on the fly.
  2. MCP Tool Integration: Exposes standard Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool contracts (retrieve_from_vault and add_to_vault).
  3. 2-Sentence Brief: Uses local embeddings and an open-weight language model to extract the exact fact and output a concise brief.

Demo

Code 

import json
import torch
import numpy as np
import gradio as gr
from transformers import pipeline
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

# 1. Load Local Open-Weight Models
embed_model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
llm_pipeline = pipeline(
    "text-generation",
    model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct",
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16 if torch.cuda.is_available() else torch.float32,
    device_map="auto" if torch.cuda.is_available() else None
)

# 2. In-Memory Vault & Seed Data
vault_docs = [
    "WiFi Password for Home Lab is 'lazy_sloth_42'. Do not share externally.",
    "Invoice #8841 from Cloud hosting was $45.20, due on November 5th.",
    "Doctor appointment rescheduled to Friday at 4:30 PM with Dr. Sharma.",
    "Project roadmap milestone 2 requires TabPFN model benchmarking by next Tuesday."
]
vault_embeddings = embed_model.encode(vault_docs)

# 3. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Tool Functions
def mcp_retrieve_from_vault(query: str, top_k: int = 2):
    global vault_docs, vault_embeddings
    if not vault_docs:
        return []
    q_vec = embed_model.encode([query])
    scores = cosine_similarity(q_vec, vault_embeddings)[0]
    top_indices = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:top_k]
    return [{"text": vault_docs[i], "similarity_score": round(float(scores[i]), 3)} for i in top_indices]

def mcp_add_to_vault(new_text: str):
    global vault_docs, vault_embeddings
    cleaned = new_text.strip()
    if not cleaned:
        return "Empty note."
    vault_docs.append(cleaned)
    new_embedding = embed_model.encode([cleaned])
    vault_embeddings = np.vstack([vault_embeddings, new_embedding])
    return f"Added to vault. Total items: {len(vault_docs)}"

# 4. Agent Synthesis
SYSTEM_PROMPT = (
    "You are SlothVault. The user is exhausted. You have executed the MCP tool "
    "'retrieve_from_vault' and received matching records. "
    "Give the exact answer in 1-2 punchy sentences. "
    "End with a short sloth remark like 'Now go back to resting. 🦥'."
)

def sloth_agent_search(query: str):
    if not query.strip():
        return "Ask something you're too lazy to search for!"

    retrieved = mcp_retrieve_from_vault(query, top_k=2)
    context_str = "\n".join([f"- {r['text']} (Match: {r['similarity_score']})" for r in retrieved])

    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": f"Query: {query}\n\nContext:\n{context_str}"}
    ]

    res = llm_pipeline(messages, max_new_tokens=120, temperature=0.2)
    answer = res[0]["generated_text"][-1]["content"].strip()

    trace = (
        f"```
{% endraw %}
json\n"
        f"// MCP Tool Execution Trace\n"
        f'{{"tool": "retrieve_from_vault", "query": "{query}", "matches": {len(retrieved)}}}\n'
        f"
{% raw %}


\n\n"
f"Retrieved Context:\n{context_str}\n\n"
f"---\n"
f"### Sloth Answer\n{answer}"
)
return trace

def handle_upload(file_obj, raw_text):
count = 0
if file_obj is not None:
with open(file_obj.name, "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore") as f:
for line in f.readlines():
if line.strip():
mcp_add_to_vault(line.strip())
count += 1
if raw_text and raw_text.strip():
mcp_add_to_vault(raw_text.strip())
count += 1
return f"Successfully ingested {count} item(s) into vault."

5. Gradio Interface

with gr.Blocks(theme=gr.themes.Soft(), title="SlothVault") as demo:
gr.Markdown("# SlothVault: Zero-Effort Local MCP + RAG Agent")
gr.Markdown("Stop organizing notes manually. Dump raw clutter and let an open-weight agent retrieve it.")

with gr.Tab(" Ask the Sloth Agent"):
    query_in = gr.Textbox(label="Ask anything:", value="What is my home lab wifi password and when is the cloud bill due?")
    search_btn = gr.Button(" Find It For Me", variant="primary")
    output_box = gr.Markdown()
    search_btn.click(fn=sloth_agent_search, inputs=query_in, outputs=output_box)

with gr.Tab(" Dump More Clutter (Add Notes)"):
    note_in = gr.Textbox(label="Paste note or snippet:", placeholder="e.g., Gate code is 8842")
    file_in = gr.File(label="Upload .txt file", file_types=[".txt"])
    add_btn = gr.Button(" Ingest Without Organizing")
    status_box = gr.Markdown()
    add_btn.click(fn=handle_upload, inputs=[file_in, note_in], outputs=status_box)

demo.launch(share=True)

How I Built It
SlothVault combines open-weight models, dense semantic retrieval, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP):

Standardized MCP Tool Contracts: Instead of building an ad-hoc search script, the data operations implement retrieve_from_vault and add_to_vault tool definitions, ensuring compatibility with standard agent frameworks.

Fast Local Vector Search: sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeds text into 384-dimensional vectors. Cosine similarity matching retrieves the top-ranked context in milliseconds without a heavy external vector database.

Local Open-Weight Reasoning: Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct synthesizes the retrieved chunks on-device, extracting precise facts and avoiding generative hallucinations.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?
Absolute Privacy: Personal notes, Wi-Fi credentials, medical reminders, and invoices never leave the machine. Running inference locally keeps sensitive personal data off third-party servers.

Zero Operating Cost: Powered by open weights, the agent runs entirely free of token limits, monthly subscriptions, or cloud API paywalls.

Offline Reliability: Because the models run on-device, the agent functions normally on a laptop even without an internet connection.

Prize Categories
Top Prize: Slow and Steady ($250 USD)

articles.title: How to Review AI-Generated Pull Requests: A Checklist Before You Merge
articles.description: A pull request can look perfect. Clean names, tidy functions, a green CI check. And half of the new...
articles.body_html:
A pull request can look perfect. Clean names, tidy functions, a green CI check. And half of the new tests can still assert nothing.

AI-written code does not look sloppy. It looks like a competent person wrote it, and that is exactly the problem. Your instincts for spotting bad code are tuned to messy code, and this is not messy.

If your team merges AI-generated code, here is a checklist to run before you do. Each item also notes what a bot can check for you, so your attention goes to the things only a human can judge.

1. Does it solve the actual problem?

AI is very good at satisfying the letter of a prompt while missing the intent. Before you read the diff, read the ticket. Write down in one sentence what this change should do.

Then look at the file list. If the ticket was about one endpoint and the pull request touches nine files, ask why. Agents love to "improve" things nobody asked them to touch.

Human's job: compare the change to the intent.
Bot's job: none. This one is yours.

2. Is the diff small enough to review?

If you cannot hold the change in your head, you cannot review it. A big AI-generated diff gets a skim and a quick approval, and that is where bugs get through.

If the diff is too large, send it back and ask for smaller pieces. This is not rude. It is the same thing you would ask of a human colleague.

Human's job: push back on size.
Bot's job: none. This one is yours.

3. Do the imports and APIs actually exist?

Generated code often calls methods or options that sound right but do not exist in your installed version. Confident-looking code is not proof.

For anything unfamiliar, check it against the official docs for the version in your lockfile. Pay special attention to new dependencies the change adds. Ask yourself whether you would have chosen that package.

Human's job: verify unfamiliar calls and new packages.
Bot's job: a dependency check can flag packages that are outdated or have known vulnerabilities, so you do not have to look each one up.

4. Do the new lines have tests, and do those tests mean anything?

This is the one that gets the least attention.

Overall coverage is a project-wide number. A pull request can add a lot of untested code and barely move it, because the old, well-tested code dilutes the result. The opposite also happens: a refactor can lower overall coverage even though the new code is fine.

What you want to know is patch coverage: of the lines this pull request changed, how many are exercised by tests? That number says much more about this specific change than the project average does.

Then check what the tests actually assert. A quick trick: flip one assertion and see whether the test still passes. If it does, the test is decoration.

// Looks like a test. Proves nothing.
test("creates a user", async () => {
  const user = await createUser({ name: "Sam" });
  expect(user).toBeDefined();
});

Human's job: read the assertions.
Bot's job: report coverage for the changed lines separately from the project total, so a gap is visible without opening a coverage report.

5. Did it copy something that already exists?

AI does not know your codebase the way you do. It often writes a new helper next to an identical one that already lives three folders away. Every copy is a place where the next bug fix has to be made twice.

Search for similar logic before approving. A new utility function should make you ask whether one already exists.

Human's job: recognize existing helpers you know about.
Bot's job: a duplication check can flag repeated blocks the pull request introduced.

6. What happens when things go wrong?

Generated code handles the happy path beautifully. Check the unhappy paths:

  • What happens with empty input or missing values?
  • What happens on a timeout or a failed network call?
  • Are errors swallowed silently? An empty catch block is a classic.
  • Does it log anything useful when it fails?

Human's job: think about failure cases.
Bot's job: a complexity check can point at functions that have grown many branches, which is where failure handling usually hides.

7. Did a secret slip in?

Agents copy examples. Sometimes an example contains something that looks like a real key, and sometimes it is one. Check for hardcoded tokens, passwords and connection strings in the diff.

Human's job: glance at config and environment changes.
Bot's job: a secrets scan on the changed lines is cheap and catches the obvious cases.

A checklist you can paste into your pull request template 

- [ ] I can state in one sentence what this change should do
- [ ] The files changed match the task
- [ ] The diff is small enough to review properly
- [ ] New imports and API calls exist in our installed versions
- [ ] New dependencies are justified, current and safe
- [ ] Changed lines have tests that fail when the code breaks
- [ ] Nothing duplicates a helper we already have
- [ ] Empty, null and failure cases are handled
- [ ] No secrets in the diff

Let a bot do the boring half

Items 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 are partly mechanical. A human reading the diff is a slow and tired way to check them, and the review energy is better spent on item 1 and on the design questions only you can answer.

DebtDraft is built for this. It is a GitHub Action that leaves one comment on each pull request with a health score across the signals above: complexity, test coverage, duplication, outdated dependencies and known-vulnerable dependencies. It also shows the changed lines on their own, so you can see what this specific pull request did, and a dashboard shows how your repository trends over time.

It is free for up to three repositories, and setup is one workflow step. If you try it, let us know what you think.

Your turn

What is the sneakiest problem you have seen in an AI-generated pull request? Share it with us in the comments.

articles.title: OpenRouter's February 2026 Outages: How a Cold Cache Overwhelmed the Database
articles.description: The database was struggling. The API said the user didn't exist.  That is the part of OpenRouter's...
articles.body_html:
The database was struggling. The API said the user didn't exist.

That is the part of OpenRouter's February outages worth looking at closely.

The reported failure involved cache connectivity and the database lookups behind API-key authentication. When the cache stopped serving those lookups, the database had to absorb work it normally wouldn't see. Requests started failing with 401 User not found.

There is an important distinction here: an authentication failure and an authentication infrastructure failure are not the same thing. If a database timeout becomes a 401, a client may treat a temporary service failure as an invalid credential. Retries, alerts and incident diagnosis can all head in the wrong direction.

The capacity problem is just as interesting. A database can appear comfortably provisioned because a cache absorbs most of the read traffic. That doesn't mean the database can survive the workload when the cache disappears. Recovery can create its own traffic spike, precisely when the dependency underneath is least able to handle it.

This is why cache-failure testing shouldn't stop at checking whether the application stays online. It should also examine database concurrency, fallback request rates, cache repopulation, retry behavior and the errors returned to clients. A fallback path that works for a few misses may behave very differently when every request takes it at once.

There is also a subtle observability problem here. The first outage coincided with a denial-of-service attack, which initially complicated the investigation. When the caching failure recurred in February without the same accompanying attack, the underlying cause became clearer. Multiple problems can overlap; temporal correlation alone doesn't establish root cause.

The remediation needs to address both load and semantics. Circuit breakers and controlled cache repopulation can limit the burst reaching the database. Returning 503 Service Unavailable rather than 401 Unauthorized when an infrastructure failure prevents an authentication lookup helps clients distinguish an unavailable service from invalid credentials.

A useful test for any cache-backed authentication system: invalidate the cache under realistic concurrency and measure the database's behavior during recovery. How quickly does load rise? Are concurrent misses coalesced? Do retries amplify the spike? Can the service shed work before the database saturates?

Those answers reveal more about the system's failure tolerance than its cache-hit ratio during normal operation.

The full postmortem reconstructs both outages, separates published facts from illustrative capacity calculations, and identifies what the available evidence does—and doesn't—establish about the remediation.

Read teh full teardown here: https://buildopsy.com/system-design/openrouter-cache-thundering-herd-postmortem.html

articles.title: Nuxt 4.6 nuxt/server: Why Mixing h3 Imports Throws NUXT_E8012
articles.description: Nuxt 4.6 added a new nuxt/server import source alongside h3 — mix the two in one handler and you hit NUXT_E8012. The real boundary, plus a cheat sheet.
articles.body_html:
A server/api/profile.get.ts handler that worked fine on Monday starts returning a NUXT_E8012 error on Tuesday, and the only thing that changed is a teammate added one line — reading the signed-in user's session with a helper imported from nuxt/server. Nothing else moved — not the route, not the defineEventHandler at the top of the file, not the dependency versions in any way you'd notice without reading package.json closely. The error message is honest about what's wrong, but only if you already know server/ now has two event shapes floating around, and that this one new line just handed a helper the wrong one.

This article is written against Nuxt 4.6, verified at v4.6.2 (the current latest on npm as of this writing; nuxt/server itself shipped in 4.6.0, released October 5, 2026, per the official GitHub release notes). If you've read the server routes episode in this series, you already know how server/api and server/middleware route a request through Nitro — this one picks up what changed on top of that in 4.6: a second, explicit way to write the exact same kind of file, and the sharp edge where the two meet.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain what nuxt/server is, why Nuxt 4.6 added it, and what it means for Nuxt to be "server-agnostic"
  • Tell apart the two coexisting ways to write server code in Nuxt 4.6 — the default h3 auto-imports and the new explicit nuxt/server imports
  • Read a NUXT_E8012 error and fix the file it's pointing at
  • Spot the subtler bug: helpers with the same name that behave differently depending on which source they came from
  • Decide whether to migrate existing server/ code now, or leave it exactly as it is

Who this is for

You've written server/api routes before — defineEventHandler, getQuery, readBody are already familiar. You don't need to have touched Nitro internals or h3 directly; this article treats the new nuxt/server import source as its own subject, not an h3 tutorial.

Table of contents

  • The problem: one new import, one confusing error
  • The mental model: two server APIs, one directory
  • Walking through it, stage by stage
  • Edge cases and gotchas
  • Best practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet
  • Key takeaways

The problem: one new import, one confusing error

Here's a server/api handler that looks like completely ordinary Nuxt 4 code, with one line added:

// server/api/profile.get.ts
import { useSession } from 'nuxt/server'

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  const id = getRouterParam(event, 'id')
  const session = useSession(event, { password: process.env.NUXT_SESSION_PASSWORD! })
  return { id, userId: session.data.userId }
})

defineEventHandler and getRouterParam in this file are untouched — still the default auto-imports, exactly as they were last week. The only new thing is one call to useSession, imported explicitly from nuxt/server, to read the signed-in user's id out of the session. Run the dev server and hit the route, and the response comes back a 500:

[nuxt] NUXT_E8012: `useSession` from `nuxt/server` was called with an h3 event. The
handler was defined with h3's `defineEventHandler` (auto-imported), which passes a
different event. Import `defineEventHandler` from `nuxt/server` alongside the helpers.

The instinct is to assume a typo, a bad auto-import, or a stale .nuxt cache — none of which is true. getRouterParam and the rest of the file's identifiers were never touched, and this isn't a build failure either — the file compiles and the dev server starts just fine. The error only shows up once the route is actually hit, because it's thrown from inside useSession itself, the moment it notices the event it was handed doesn't look like the one nuxt/server expects. That's the whole bug: a handler still built with h3's own defineEventHandler handed one of nuxt/server's session helpers an event it can't work with — and it's also, it turns out, a deliberate guardrail rather than a bug at all.

The mental model: two server APIs, one directory

Before 4.6, server/ had exactly one API: a set of h3 and Nitro helpers (defineEventHandler, getQuery, readBody, getRouterParam, createError, and so on) that Nuxt auto-imports into every file under server/. That hasn't gone away — the release notes are explicit that the auto-imported helpers "are still h3's own helpers," unchanged, and nothing in the 4.6 release requires you to touch them.

What 4.6 adds is nuxt/server — a second, explicit import source, described as "a complement to nuxt/app." Most of what it exports — getQuery, readBody, getRouterParam, and friends — are the exact same underlying h3/Nitro functions, re-exported under a new door, so importing them explicitly from nuxt/server instead of relying on the auto-import changes nothing about how they behave. A few exports are genuinely different, though: nuxt/server ships its own defineEventHandler (the one that builds the portable RequestEvent, with web-standard shape like event.req and event.res.headers), its own createError and sendRedirect with different contracts (more on those below), and its own session API — useSession, getSession, updateSession, clearSession — built specifically to read and write session data off that portable event.

That session API is the clearest place NUXT_E8012 shows up. Each of those four helpers checks the event it's handed: if it looks like an h3 v1 event (no .req, just the legacy node request/response pair) rather than nuxt/server's own event, it throws NUXT_E8012, naming the helper and telling you to import defineEventHandler from nuxt/server too. That only happens if the handler around it is still built with the auto-imported defineEventHandler — the one that still produces an h3 v1 event. Reach for useSession (or one of its three siblings) inside a handler like that, and the event shape it's handed doesn't match what the helper needs. The session helpers aren't the only ones that check — the release notes describe the error more broadly, as something you'll hit from mixing the two import sources in general, so treat the session API as the headline example, not an exhaustive list.

The reason nuxt/server exists at all is the headline of the release: Nuxt is moving toward being server-agnostic — not tied to Nitro as the only possible engine underneath server/. A handler built end-to-end on nuxt/server's portable event is meant to run unchanged whether the engine underneath it is Nitro, or the new experimental @nuxt/vite-server, or — per the release notes — Nitro v3 and h3 v2 once Nuxt 5 ships. Nitro itself isn't going anywhere; the same notes call it "still the right choice for almost everyone," including for 4.6.

Key concept: in this episode's example, NUXT_E8012 comes from nuxt/server's session helpers refusing to work with an event they can't read, because the handler around them never opted into the portable event that makes them work — getQuery, readBody, and getRouterParam don't care which defineEventHandler built the event, so pairing those with the auto-import doesn't trip it. The release notes frame the error more generally, as something mixing the two import sources can produce, so don't assume every other helper is exempt just because these three are.

Walking through it, stage by stage

Stage 1 — the default path needs nothing from you

If you've never heard of nuxt/server, your existing server/api, server/routes, and server/middleware files are unaffected by 4.6. The auto-imported defineEventHandler, getQuery, readBody, getRouterParam, and createError are exactly the h3 helpers they always were. Upgrading to 4.6 changes nothing here — this is the whole point of the release notes' line that "nothing in this release requires a migration."

Stage 2 — opting in, one file at a time

To build a handler around the portable event — and unlock nuxt/server's own defineEventHandler, createError, sendRedirect, and session helpers — you import explicitly, by name, from nuxt/server:

// server/api/health.get.ts — fully opted in
import { defineEventHandler, getQuery, useSession } from 'nuxt/server'

export default defineEventHandler(async (event) => {
  const { verbose } = getQuery(event)
  const session = await useSession(event, { password: process.env.NUXT_SESSION_PASSWORD! })
  return { ok: true, verbose: verbose === 'true', userId: session.data.userId }
})

Because defineEventHandler here is nuxt/server's own version, the event it builds has .req on it — exactly the shape useSession checks for. getQuery behaves identically either way (it's the same h3 helper regardless of source), but the handler itself is opted all the way in, which is what the session API actually needs.

Stage 3 — what actually trips NUXT_E8012

This is the pairing from the mental model above, put to use: switch the handler's defineEventHandler to the nuxt/server import too, and the session helper gets the portable event it's checking for.

// fixed — defineEventHandler now comes from nuxt/server as well
import { defineEventHandler, getRouterParam, useSession } from 'nuxt/server'

export default defineEventHandler(async (event) => {
  const id = getRouterParam(event, 'id')
  const session = await useSession(event, { password: process.env.NUXT_SESSION_PASSWORD! })
  return { id, userId: session.data.userId }
})

Notice what doesn't need to change to clear the error: getRouterParam was never what threw NUXT_E8012, whether it came from the auto-import or from nuxt/server — it doesn't check which defineEventHandler built the event the way the session helpers do. The one identifier that has to move to fix this error is defineEventHandler itself, because that's what decides which event shape every helper in the handler gets handed. getRouterParam itself behaves the same from either source, for what it's worth — see the next section for the helpers that actually do differ.

Stage 4 — the quieter trap: same name, different contract

A couple of helpers behave differently depending on which source they came from, and none of these trip NUXT_E8012 either — that error is specific to the session API, not to these. nuxt/server's sendRedirect still sets the response status and Location header as a side effect, exactly like the auto-imported one — but instead of ending the response there, it also returns an HTML <meta http-equiv="refresh"> body as a fallback for a client that ignores the status code (inspecting the installed nuxt@4.6.2 package directly: dist/server/index.js's sendRedirect calls setResponseStatus(event, status) and event.res.headers.set('location', location) before returning that HTML string). So the redirect itself — the part every browser and fetch call actually relies on — works whether or not the handler returns that value; skipping the return only drops the fallback body, which matters solely to a user agent that ignores both the status and the header. Its createError takes status and statusText, where the h3-helper createError you already know takes statusCode and statusMessage — though nuxt/server's createError still accepts statusCode/statusMessage too, as deprecated aliases, so that direction keeps working. And response headers go through event.res.headers, a web-standard Headers-shaped object, rather than h3 v1's own header-setting helpers.

// h3-style (auto-imported) — sends the full response immediately as a side effect
export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  return sendRedirect(event, '/login')
})

// nuxt/server-style — sets status + Location immediately too, then returns a fallback body
import { defineEventHandler, sendRedirect } from 'nuxt/server'

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  sendRedirect(event, '/login')
  // no `return` here — the 302 and Location header are already set, so the
  // redirect still happens; only the <meta refresh> fallback page is skipped
})

Neither example throws NUXT_E8012 — that error only ever comes from the session helpers, never from sendRedirect. The real gotcha here is narrower than it looks: dropping the return doesn't break the redirect, it just means a browser gets an empty body alongside the 302 instead of the fallback HTML. Worth knowing, but not worth losing an afternoon over — the loud NUXT_E8012 error from the session helpers is still the one that actually blocks a request.

Stage 5 — deciding whether to opt in at all

Nothing forces you to touch nuxt/server today. The case for doing it anyway, per the release notes, is forward-looking: Nuxt 5 will move to Nitro v3 and h3 v2, and server code written against nuxt/server on 4.6 "runs unchanged there." Code left on the auto-imported h3 helpers isn't broken by this — it keeps working exactly as it did on Nuxt 4.5 — but it's the code that will need attention whenever that migration comes. If you're starting a new server/ file today and have no reason to care about portability, the auto-imports remain the simpler, fully-supported default. If you're building something you expect to still be maintaining past the next major, nuxt/server is the version of "write it once" that this release is actually offering.

Edge cases and gotchas

It's not a per-project switch — it's per call. You can have some server/ files on the auto-imports and others fully on nuxt/server in the same project; most helpers don't care which source built the event they're handed. Only a session-helper call cares, and only at the moment it runs — importing useSession and never calling it is harmless, since the check happens inside the helper itself, not from a static scan of the file's imports.

@nuxt/vite-server is explicitly experimental. The release notes introduce it alongside nuxt/server as a second, pure-Vite server builder, but they're equally explicit that "Nitro is still the right choice for almost everyone" right now. Treat it as a preview of where server-agnostic Nuxt is headed, not a production alternative to reach for in 4.6.

Server-side useState/useRoute still don't belong in either server API. Nothing about nuxt/server changes the boundary the server routes episode in this series covers — both the h3-auto-import world and the nuxt/server world are still the Nitro/h3 side of the project, with no Vue application instance for a composable to attach to.

Best practices

  • If a handler calls useSession, getSession, updateSession, or clearSession, make sure that same handler's defineEventHandler is imported from nuxt/server too. That pairing is the one thing NUXT_E8012 actually enforces — get it right and the rest of the file's imports (auto-imported or explicit) don't matter to this particular error.
  • Don't migrate existing files just because 4.6 shipped. The release notes are explicit that nothing requires it; migrate a file when you have an actual reason (adopting the session API, building for a new server builder, preparing early for Nuxt 5), not as busywork.
  • When you do reach for nuxt/server's own helpers, re-check the contract — not just sendRedirect and createError, but anything that used to write directly to the response. The upgrade guide's comparison table is the source of truth, not assumption-by-familiar-name.
  • If a NUXT_E8012 shows up in a file you didn't expect, look for a call to useSession/getSession/updateSession/clearSession and check what built the event around it — it's almost always a defineEventHandler that's still the h3 auto-import.

FAQ

Do I have to migrate my existing server/ code to nuxt/server?

No. The 4.6 release notes say directly that nothing in the release requires a migration — files using only the auto-imported h3 helpers keep working exactly as they did on 4.5.

What exactly causes a NUXT_E8012 error?

Calling one of nuxt/server's session helpers — useSession, getSession, updateSession, or clearSession — inside a handler whose defineEventHandler is still the default auto-import. The helper gets handed an h3 v1 event instead of the portable one it needs, and throws at request time, naming itself in the error. It's not a build-time check and it's not about any other helper pairing — getQuery, readBody, and getRouterParam behave identically no matter which source you import them from.

Is nuxt/server replacing Nitro?

No. Nitro remains the default engine underneath both import styles in 4.6, and the release notes call it "still the right choice for almost everyone." nuxt/server is a portable way to write handlers that happen to run on Nitro today and could run on a different server builder later — it isn't a replacement for Nitro itself.

Do sendRedirect, createError, and getRouterParam behave the same regardless of where I import them from?

Mostly, but not entirely. getRouterParam/getRouterParams behave identically either way — both default to the raw, undecoded route segment, and both accept { decode: true } to decode it. createError does differ: nuxt/server's version takes status/statusText (it still accepts statusCode/statusMessage too, as deprecated aliases), while the auto-imported h3 helper only recognizes statusCode/statusMessage. sendRedirect sets the status and Location header as a side effect either way, then additionally returns a <meta refresh> fallback body from the nuxt/server version — skip the return and the redirect still happens, you just lose that fallback body. None of this is NUXT_E8012, which comes only from the session API checking the event shape it's handed.

Should I use @nuxt/vite-server instead of Nitro?

Not yet, for anything you're shipping. The release notes introduce it as experimental, in the same breath as recommending Nitro for almost everyone. It's worth knowing it exists as a sign of where Nuxt's server layer is heading, not as a current production choice.

Cheat sheet

Situation What to do
New server/ file, no portability need Leave it on the default auto-imports — no import needed
Want a handler portable beyond Nitro Import everything server-related in that file from nuxt/server
Calling getQuery/readBody from either source Behaves identically — they're the same h3 helper either way
Calling getRouterParam/getRouterParams from either source Behaves identically — both default to the raw, undecoded segment; pass { decode: true } on either to decode it
Calling useSession/getSession/updateSession/clearSession Only works if that handler's defineEventHandler is also from nuxt/server
NUXT_E8012 in a file you didn't expect Find the session-helper call and check whether its handler still uses the auto-imported defineEventHandler
Redirecting with the auto-imported sendRedirect Just call it — it ends the response immediately as a side effect
Redirecting with nuxt/server's sendRedirect Sets status + Location immediately too; return sendRedirect(event, path) additionally sends a fallback body for clients that ignore the status
Throwing with the auto-imported createError { statusCode, statusMessage }
Throwing with nuxt/server's createError { status, statusText }
Deciding whether to migrate at all Only if you have a real reason — nothing requires it on 4.6
Trying @nuxt/vite-server Experimental — fine to explore, not yet for production

Key takeaways

  • Nuxt 4.6 added nuxt/server, a new explicit import source for server code, alongside the default auto-imported h3 helpers that server/ has always had — most of what it exports is the same h3/Nitro functions under a new door, not a parallel implementation.
  • NUXT_E8012 is narrower than "don't mix imports": it fires specifically when nuxt/server's session helpers (useSession, getSession, updateSession, clearSession) are called inside a handler whose defineEventHandler is still the auto-import — the fix is pairing that one import with nuxt/server too.
  • createError shares a name across both sources but not a contract (status/statusText vs. statusCode/statusMessage), and sendRedirect sets its status and Location header the same way in both but only returns a fallback body from nuxt/server — skipping that return loses the fallback body, not the redirect. getRouterParam/getRouterParams behave identically from either source. None of these throw NUXT_E8012.
  • Migrating existing code to nuxt/server is optional today, and mainly worth it if you want a handler to keep working unchanged once Nuxt 5 moves to Nitro v3 and h3 v2.

The teammate's one-line import, explained

That NUXT_E8012 from the top of the article wasn't a cache problem or a typo — it was nuxt/server's session API refusing to read a session off an event it doesn't recognize. Once you know the error belongs specifically to the session helpers, not to every helper in the file, it stops looking like a mystery and starts looking like a guardrail with a narrow, specific job — and the subtler case, the same-named helper that behaves differently with no error at all, is the one worth remembering long after a request stops failing.

articles.title: AI agents were told my inputs were optional, then rejected for leaving them out 🤖
articles.description: One word in 29 config files: required. Every field it guarded already had a default.  Hi! I'm Tim, a...
articles.body_html:
One word in 29 config files: required. Every field it guarded already had a default.

Hi! I'm Tim, a self-taught developer in Nairobi. I build small data tools that run as Apify Actors, serverless jobs that people pay for per result. 100 of them are public.

This week Apify's DEV account published What AI agents see when they call your Apify Actors, by SIÁN Agency. One finding in it sent me straight to my own input schemas.

🤖 What an agent sees

A person runs an Actor from a form. The fields have labels, the dropdowns list the valid values, and an example is already filled in.

An AI agent connected through the Apify MCP server gets none of that. It gets the input schema as JSON Schema, and it sends what the schema says.

The article found that two parts of the MCP server read that schema differently:

  • tools/list tells the model what a tool accepts. It leaves a field out of required when that field has a default.
  • tools/call checks the model's arguments. It validates against the original schema and doesn't fill in defaults first.

So a field that is both required and has a default is listed as optional. When the model leaves it out, the call is rejected with a validation error (-32602) for the very field it was told it could skip.

An agent can recover by fetching the Actor's details and trying again. It still burns a round trip on the first call, every time. The author found this in 59 of the 253 schemas they checked.

🔍 How many of mine?

I wrote a short script that reads every .actor/input_schema.json in my portfolio. For each required field, it records whether the field has a default and whether that default equals the prefill, the example shown in the form.

Count
Actors with at least one required field 29 of 100
Required fields that also had a default 32, in 26 Actors
Required fields with no default 3, in 3 Actors
Defaults identical to the prefill 32 of 32

Here's a typical one, from a vehicle safety ratings lookup (trimmed to the parts that matter):

{
    "required": ["year", "make", "model"],
    "properties": {
        "year":  { "type": "integer", "prefill": 2022,     "default": 2022 },
        "make":  { "type": "string",  "prefill": "Honda",  "default": "Honda" },
        "model": { "type": "string",  "prefill": "Accord", "default": "Accord" }
    }
}

All three fields are required, and all three have a default. In the form, nothing looks wrong, because the form is already filled in. To an agent, all three are listed as optional, and a call without them fails.

🙈 Why nothing ever caught it

Apify runs every public Actor once a day with its prefilled input, and flags it if that run fails three days in a row.

All 32 defaults were identical to the prefill. So the daily test always sent every required field, and it always passed. None of these Actors was ever flagged for it.

The test walks the path a person takes. An agent sending {} takes a different one, and nothing was walking it.

🚫 Why I didn't run the probe

The article comes with a probe that calls each Actor through the MCP server with {}. I didn't run it on mine. My own runs show up in my Actors' analytics as a user, and that analytics page is the only signal I have about real customers, so I debug locally and keep platform runs to a minimum.

That left the static half: what the schemas say. The article is clear that this half can't find everything. An Actor can report SUCCEEDED with nothing useful in it, and only running it shows that. So after the schemas, I read through the code paths of my best-earning Actor by hand, looking for that kind of silent result. More on that in fix 3.

🔧 Fix 1: a field with a default doesn't need required

Apify writes schema defaults into every run's input. A required field with a default is filled in whether the caller sends it or not, so the required flag adds nothing to the run. All it does is mislead the agent.

The rule I applied to the 26 Actors:

// Drop `required` only when every required field already has a default.
const noDefault = schema.required.filter((k) => schema.properties[k].default === undefined);
if (noDefault.length) throw new Error(`no default for ${noDefault.join(', ')}`);
schema.required = [];

Nothing else in any schema changed, and the script checked that too. A person in the form sees exactly the same thing as before.

🔧 Fix 2: three fields had no default at all

A court opinion search (query), a travel per diem lookup (locations) and a package health check (packages) each had a required field with no default.

These were honest: with no default, nothing gets dropped from the tool listing, so an agent is told to send the field. But their code also threw on empty input:

if (!query) {
    throw new Error('query is required.');
}

I wanted every one of my Actors to answer {} the same way: with the example from the form, not an error. Each of the three got a default equal to its prefill, and the code now falls back to that example:

// An empty call (an AI agent calling with {}, or an empty API call) searches the input form's example instead of failing.
const query = String(queryInput ?? '').trim() || 'antitrust';
if (!String(queryInput ?? '').trim()) log.info('No query given, so searching the example "antitrust".');

In the two that take a list, a value that isn't a list still fails with a clear message. Only "nothing at all" falls back to the example.

🔇 Fix 3: zero rows is not an answer

My best-earning Actor audits small business websites and scores each business as a lead for web designers. It has a filter: only keep businesses that score above a minimum.

Set that minimum high enough and every business gets filtered out. The run used to end SUCCEEDED, with zero rows. An agent reading that would tell its user "no leads found", as a fact about the world. The real answer was "your filter was stricter than every business it checked".

And an empty call ({}) used to fail outright with "Nothing to audit", even though the schema told an agent nothing was required. Now it audits the three example businesses from the form.

For the empty case, a run that saves nothing now saves one row explaining why, and doesn't charge for it:

// Never end with an empty dataset: say why nothing was saved, in one uncharged row.
if (stats.pushed === 0) {
    const note = emptyRunNote(stats, counters, options, search, categoryTitle);
    await Actor.pushData(note);
}

Here's the row it writes when the filter removes all 5 businesses it audited:

{
    "name": "No businesses saved in this run (not charged)",
    "websiteStatus": null,
    "opportunityScore": null,
    "note": "All 5 businesses audited scored below 100, so none were saved (filtered businesses aren't charged). Lower minScore or turn off onlyOpportunities to see them.",
    "processed": 5,
    "filteredOut": 5
}

The row says what happened and what to change. A person can read that. So can a model.

🚀 Shipping 29 Actors, one at a time

29 Actors meant 29 builds. I didn't want a loop that pushes everything and checks nothing, so each Actor went through the same steps, and the script stopped at the first problem (trimmed):

before=$(node live-build.js "$a")            # the build to roll back to
git commit -q -m "$msg" && git push -q origin HEAD
out=$(timeout 480 apify push 2>&1)
echo "$out" | grep -q "Build: SUCCEEDED" || { echo "STOP $a"; exit 1; }
verify=$(node live-build.js "$a" --verify)   # live schema: required is [] and matches local
echo "OK $a | before $before | after $verify"

The --verify step reads the input schema back from the new live build, not from my disk. All 29 passed, and the previous build of every Actor is saved in case one needs rolling back.

🎯 What I learned

  • My input schemas have a second reader now. I wrote them for a form. A model reads them as a contract, and a contradiction in the contract becomes a failed call.
  • required plus default is a contradiction. If the platform fills a field in anyway, don't tell callers they must send it.
  • A daily test only checks the path it takes. Passing it says nothing about any other input, including an empty one.
  • Zero rows needs a reason. If a filter removes everything, say so in a row, not in a log nobody opens.
  • There's more to check. 33 fields across 16 of my Actors still have a prefill but no default. A person sees the example. An agent sending {} gets nothing for that field. Some of those Actors already fall back to an example in code; I haven't checked the rest yet.

If you publish Actors, this one-liner lists the fields in a schema that are both required and defaulted:

node -e "const s=require('./.actor/input_schema.json');console.log((s.required||[]).filter(k=>s.properties[k]?.default!==undefined))"

An empty list means an agent gets an honest contract. Anything else is a field it was told it could skip, and then got rejected for skipping.

articles.title: How I kept two docs sites apart in one WordPress install (and almost gave up)
articles.description: I already had the BeeEngine docs on beeenginejs.com as static WordPress pages. When BeeLadybug grew...
articles.body_html:
I already had the BeeEngine docs on beeenginejs.com as static WordPress pages. When BeeLadybug grew big enough to need its own docs, about 33 pages, I hit a wall. Everything I made ended up mixed in with the BeeEngine pages: the same page list, the same hierarchy, the same mess. Using posts wasn't an option either, because docs aren't blog articles.

I'll be honest: I was close to dropping it. I'm not a WordPress plugin expert, and every solution I found was either too complicated or broke something else.

The fix: a custom post type

The answer turned out to be simple. I gave BeeLadybug its own content type:

  1. I installed Custom Post Type UI.
  2. I created a post type with the slug ladybug, set Hierarchical to true and Has archive to false.
  3. I went to Settings → Permalinks and clicked Save. Skip this step and you'll get 404s.

Now every BeeLadybug page lives under /ladybug/... with its own URL, and it's completely separate from the BeeEngine pages in the admin.

Keeping the style separate too

Each page is a Custom HTML block, and all the CSS is scoped under a .bld-docs wrapper, so it never leaks into the theme or the BeeEngine docs. Links to pages I haven't written yet point to # and get dimmed:

.bld-docs a[href="#"] {
  opacity: .4;
  pointer-events: none;
}

What I learned

The problem was never WordPress, it was not knowing which tool to use. If you're stuck on something similar, keep going. The fix might be one plugin and one checkbox away.🫈🫈🫈
